newsitem.title: USA: Calif. Gov. asks Clinton for aid with flood funds.
newsitem.headline: Calif. Gov. asks Clinton for aid with flood funds.

text.p: California Gov. Pete Wilson appealed Thursday to the federal government to quickly provide hundreds of millions of dollars to help repair flood-damaged levees, roads and buildings in the state.

"I call on President Clinton to do all he can from Washington," Wilson, a Republican, said in a statement. "I trust that in this time of need, the White House and Congress will do what's fair for California and not shortchange us on disaster relief."

In a letter to Clinton Thursday, Wilson requested that the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers restore damaged flood control facilities to their pre-flood capacities and asked Clinton to direct the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to implement emergency measures to help speed up levee repairs.
The governor also called on Clinton to include funding in the federal supplemental appropriations bill to address the costs of levee repair, transportation and public assistance.
"Repair to our damaged levee system is urgently needed to protect the lives, property, and water supply for millions of Californians," Wilson said in his letter to Clinton.

The governor said the Corps of Engineers, primarily responsible for levee repairs, will need over $300 million to repair damage from the January floods. Wilson said damage estimates may increase as more information becomes available.
Wilson said the state's transportation system was "devastated" in some areas by the flooding and he estimated that $381 million would be required to fund the federal share of roadway repairs.
"It is imperative that the Federal Highway Administration have sufficient funding available to provide assistance as they have in previous disasters," Wilson said.
In addition, Wilson said at least $200 million would be needed to fund the federal share of repairs to public facilities and schools, and to fund grants for families.
Under current law, the Federal Emergency Management Agency pays 75 percent of certain costs of repairing damaged public facilities and providing assistance to flood victims.
Damages from the January floods were estimated at over $1.5 billion, state officials said. The floods damaged thousands of homes and businesses and inundated tens of thousands of acres of farmland.
